title: Why We Disappear: What Twenty Years in the Executive Suite Taught Me About Childhood
author: John R. Miles
source: petergray.substack.com (Play Makes Us Human, guest post), October 4, 2026
summary: In this guest post on Peter Gray's Substack, former executive John R. Miles argues that many high performers do not suffer burnout so much as a mattering crisis. He opens with a senior leader, David, who was indispensable at work yet had stopped offering ideas, preferences or challenges, and who believed he would be replaced within a day of dying at his desk. Drawing on Isaac Prilleltensky, Miles distinguishes belonging (having a place) from mattering (feeling valued and adding value). He suggests the pattern starts in conditional schooling, where ranking and test scores teach children to hide or to perform for approval, and cites Suniya Luthar's finding that pressure rather than affluence harms teens. The workplace then rewards the same lessons. His remedies are regard that is not contingent on output, real self-direction, and unmanaged time, illustrated by David's children placing a painted brick on the table to cue him to stop commanding and simply be present.
points: Miles separates belonging from mattering: belonging says you have a place, while mattering asks whether the room would be different without you.
He calls the pattern the Slow Fade, in which a reliable performer keeps complying and hitting numbers while his own voice and needs disappear.
The author traces the problem back to conditional schooling, where comparison and ranking teach children that worth depends on achievement.
Luthar's research is used as evidence that pressure, not affluence, drives anxiety and depression among teens, and that unconditional enjoyment protects them.
The leader's fixes mirror the child's fixes: non-contingent regard, a decision that is genuinely theirs, and unclaimed time, sometimes literally a brick on the table.
quotes: Belonging says I have a place here. Mattering has two sides, feeling valued and adding value, and it asks a harder question: would this room be different if I weren’t in it?
This is what I would call the Slow Fade: keep showing up, keep complying, keep hitting all the numbers while everything you say or need gets drowned out.
He was delivering flawless utility, but the human being inside the role had quietly checked out.
Mattering isn’t mainly something adults deliver to children by approving of them. It grows out of being trusted to act and seeing that your actions have consequences.

She found that affluence itself was not the cause, pressure was. The fortunate teens were those whose parents, whether wealthy or not, didn’t care about the grades and enjoyed their children just as they were.

The ones that disappeared were seldom bad workers. They were more often the good workers, who did more than their share, never said no, and quietly accepted their disappearance as an entity beyond their achievements.
Most could tell me how their work was assessed, but few could tell me what they’d do if no one assessed them.
A life isn’t remade by a single grand act. It is remade in the same manner it was worn down. Mattering grows through repeated evidence.
